comparison: Perfect agreement on generalization findings (C6, C48-C55). Both evaluations confirm that fish successfully generalized the learned rule to novel situations across multiple dimensions (height, size, speed). OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence from first trials, while peer reviewers highlight this as convincing evidence of rule learning with preserved decision speed.

Strong agreement on dual-rule usage (C7, C56-C64, plus C65-C67 from peer). Both evaluations accept that fish can simultaneously maintain different rules for different shapes. Peer reviewer describes this as 'a remarkable finding' and OpenEval confirms statistical evidence for parallel rule implementation without specialization by individual fish.

Disagreement on VR system validation (C30-C37). OpenEval finds comprehensive validation through controls and statistical equivalence. Peer Reviewer 2 raises significant technical concerns about stimulus continuity at 120 FPS and questions experimental design, though Reviewer 3 praises the setup. After revision, concerns remain partially unresolved.

Major disagreement on decision speed claims (C8, C19, C74). OpenEval accepts the 40 ms reaction time based on current and cited measurements. Peer Reviewer 2 directly challenges this, citing previous studies showing 60-75 ms and calling the 40 ms claim 'overselling the result.' Editor accepts 'very rapid (less than 100 ms)' but specific 40 ms claim remains contested.

Agreement on behavioral reprogramming (C5, C42, C47, C68). Both evaluations accept that fish successfully learned new rules and can modulate fast responses. OpenEval emphasizes extensive training data and controls ruling out alternative explanations. Peer reviewers confirm adaptation to different simulated physics, though debate whether speed qualifies as truly reflex-like.

Agreement on maintained speed without speed-accuracy tradeoff (C40, C41, C46). Both evaluations confirm that reprogrammed decisions maintain response characteristics and speed. Peer reviewers accept that novel situations 'preserve the speed of the fish's decision' and no reviewer challenges the absence of speed-accuracy tradeoff.

Agreement on rapid rule selection (C65-C67). Both evaluations accept that shape processing and rule selection occur within the rapid decision window. OpenEval emphasizes statistical equivalence between prior information and motion-onset-only conditions. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their acceptance of dual-rule findings.

Disagreement on control experiments (C33-C34, C43-C44). OpenEval finds these controls demonstrate fish respond to screen motion rather than feeders. Peer Reviewer 2 questions whether fish truly perceive virtual targets as falling targets, asking 'How do authors validate that the fish indeed perceives the virtual target as falling target?' This fundamental concern about perception remains partially unresolved.

Agreement on spatial generalization (C45). Both evaluations accept that learned behavior generalizes across different starting positions and orientations. This is part of the broader generalization findings that peer reviewers explicitly endorse as part of 'a variety of novel situations.'

Partial disagreement on methodological adequacy (C94). OpenEval treats experimental details as straightforward factual statements. Peer Reviewer 3 raises concerns about sample size (6 fish) and individual variability, requesting information about consistency across individuals, which is 'essential for appreciating the flexibility of the system.'
